title: A finite window cannot cure an infinite total
question: What happens if every radiation mode receives classical thermal energy?
recap: At a positive temperature, classical allocation assigns more energy as the frequency cutoff rises. Its all-frequency total has no finite value; the plotting cutoff is not a physical explanation.
premises: Classical equilibrium assigns mean energy k_B T to each radiation mode.
The number of modes per unit volume per unit frequency grows as frequency squared.
limitations: The allocation is a classical model, not the measured all-frequency spectrum.
A finite cutoff is a declared calculation boundary, not an inferred property of light.

overview.text: At a positive temperature, classical allocation assigns more energy as the frequency cutoff rises. Its all-frequency total has no finite value; the plotting cutoff is not a physical explanation.

full.text: Counting cavity modes and giving each mode the classical mean energy k_B T produces a spectral energy density uν. A density must be multiplied by a frequency width to give energy per unit volume.

full.spoken: The classical energy density per unit frequency is eight pi frequency squared times thermal energy, divided by light speed cubed.
The energy density below cutoff frequency nu c is eight pi k B T over three c cubed, times cutoff frequency cubed.

full.text: At fixed positive temperature, doubling the cutoff multiplies this finite-range total by eight. Extending the model to arbitrarily high frequencies produces an unbounded total. LQ-02 keeps that failure distinct from the finite portion displayed on screen.

full.returnCaption: Return to integrating a spectral density over a stated frequency range.

items: Specify a positive equilibrium temperature and a finite cutoff frequency.
Multiply mode density 8πν²/c³ by mean mode energy k_B T.
Integrate ν² from zero to the cutoff; its integral is the cutoff cubed divided by three.
Compare two cutoffs while keeping temperature fixed: a factor two in cutoff gives a factor eight in total.
Let the cutoff increase without bound. There is no finite limiting total to plot.
Do not interpret a numerical refusal at infinite cutoff as zero energy.

margin.text: k_B and c are modern explanatory notation. The paper writes R/N for the thermal constant and L for the speed of light. Historical names and later terminology are not additional evidence for the model.
